newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Financial reform hopes push Seoul shrs to close up.
newsitem.headline: Financial reform hopes push Seoul shrs to close up.

text.p: Shares ended higher for the third consecutive day on Friday, boosted by the government's intention to reform the financial industry and lower interest rates, brokers said.
Hopes for active mergers and acquisitions in the financial sectors and imminent market boosting measures were supporting the rises, they added.
The composite stock index provisionally ended at 648.69. 8.82 points higher.
"The government has said it has the will to reform, but now it has to show specifics," said a Dongsuh Securities broker.
"If the government doesn't meet the expectations, there's a big possibility for another fall," he added.

Market sentiment improved following President Kim Young-sam's New Year news conference on Tuesday, when Kim said a committee on financial reform would be established and priority put on lowering interest rates.

Brokers said the rises were being tempered by worries that labour unrest would worsen next week. "If the strike situation becomes more complicated and drags out, it's not going to be good for the economy," said Rhee Joo-ik of Daewoo Securities.

Nationwide strikes, spearheaded by the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, erupted on December 26 in protest at the passage of a controversial new labour bill that allows employers to lay-off workers.
The nation's largest union group, the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, called on workers to participate in the industrial action for two days starting next Tuesday.
Brokers said the labour unrest situation would have major impact on the market next week. "If the strikes are serious, manufacturing stocks will weaken and banks regain strength," said Rhee.

Heavily market-weighted blue chip shares profited on Friday's improved sentiment. KEPCO rose 1,000 won to 27,100, Korea Mobile Telecom gained 16,000 won to 447,000, and Samsung Electronics climbed 300 won to 42,300.
Bank shares, which had climbed nearly 20 percent over the past several days, were hit by profit-taking.
Korea Exchange Bank fell 270 won to 8,950, Commercial Bank lost 10 won to 6,100 and Cho Hung Bank shed 60 won to 6,950.
SEOULBANK, however, maintained its position as most actively traded stock, rising 130 won to 4,900.
